name: context_distillation
description: Efficient LLM Context Distillation - CS 7643 Deep Learning Project comparing vanilla vs pattern-based fine-tuning approaches for natural language understanding

readme.html:
Context distillation on small OPT models

A four-person course project for CS 7643 (Deep Learning) at Georgia Tech, spring 2024. The question: when a small language model learns a sentence-pair task from only 16 examples, does context distillation keep it more accurate on out-of-domain data than ordinary fine-tuning does? In these experiments it did not. Context distillation gave no gain over the other methods and was slower to train.

The full report is Efficient_LLM_Context_Distillation-CS_7643.pdf. The results below come from the report. The description of the code comes from the code itself and from a test run of both scripts.

What was compared

Five ways to adapt Meta's OPT models (125M, 350M and 1.3B parameters) to a task, each from 16 training examples:

Method What it trains
Vanilla fine-tuning the whole model, with a new two-class classifier head in place of the language-model head
Pattern-based fine-tuning (PBFT) the whole model; the language-model head predicts a label token after a fixed prompt pattern
In-context learning (ICL) nothing; the examples go into the prompt
Context distillation PBFT's task loss plus a context loss: the pre-trained model's top 50 logits at each token of general-purpose text (Alpaca), matched with binary cross-entropy. Total loss = 0.9 × task + 0.1 × context, the best weighting tried
BitFit only the bias terms

Each task has an in-domain dataset for training and validation and an out-of-domain (OOD) dataset of the same kind:

In-domain Out-of-domain
QQP (are two questions duplicates?) PAWS-QQP
MNLI (does one sentence entail another?) HANS
RTE (entailment) HANS

Every fine-tuning run trained for 40 epochs and kept the checkpoint with the best in-domain validation accuracy. The learning rate and the other training settings came from the PBFT paper. The team aimed for five seeds per configuration; memory limits, crashes and time left some with fewer (table below).

Result: no gain from context distillation

From section 3 of the report:

  • Accuracy is 50–60 % almost everywhere, only a little above chance. QQP and PAWS-QQP are the two unbalanced sets: QQP is 40 % duplicates, so answering "not a duplicate" every time scores 60 %; PAWS-QQP is 28 % duplicates, so the same answer scores 72 % there. On QQP no method differs significantly from another.
  • MNLI: PBFT reaches significantly higher in-domain accuracy than the other methods at 350M and 1.3B. The authors' reading: the learning rate came from the PBFT paper, so it suits PBFT best.
  • RTE: no method stands out, and most sit near chance. Context distillation scores above BitFit, but it has only one seed at 350M and at 1.3B, so that gap may be chance.
  • Overall: no evidence that context distillation helps at these sizes. It is also much slower to train, because its loss backpropagates through the top 50 logits at every token instead of one label token. The report recommends PBFT in most cases.

Limits the report names: models stop at 1.3B, and the PBFT paper sees most of the separation between methods at larger sizes. Context distillation used one loss weighting and one learning rate for every model and dataset, and took its context loss from one general dataset.

Figures 2–4 of the report plot each configuration's mean OOD accuracy against its in-domain accuracy, one panel per task. Figures 5–7 plot every run.

Completed seeds per configuration (Figure 1 of the report; a dash means none ran):

Method MNLI 125M MNLI 350M MNLI 1.3B QQP 125M QQP 350M QQP 1.3B RTE 125M RTE 350M RTE 1.3B
Vanilla fine-tuning 5 5 5 6 5 5 5 5 5
PBFT 5 5 5 6 5 5 1 1 5
ICL 5 5 1 5 5 2 5 5 –
Context distillation 5 5 5 1 5 5 5 1 1
BitFit 5 5 5 5 5 5 5 5 5

What is in this repository

This repository holds the RTE part of the code: vanilla fine-tuning and PBFT on RTE, scored out of domain on HANS. The QQP and MNLI scripts and the ICL, context distillation and BitFit code are not here, so the report's results cannot be rerun from this repository alone.

File What it does
vanilla_ft_rte.py vanilla fine-tuning on RTE (AutoModelForSequenceClassification, Adafactor optimiser)
pattern_based_ft_rte.py PBFT on RTE: an OPTForCausalLM wrapper, adapted from the PBFT paper's code (uds-lsv/llmft), that reads the next-token logits at the last non-padding token; the Trainer's default AdamW optimiser
utils.py seeding, run folder names, training with its log written to a file, and get_data_from_approach(), which loads finished runs into pandas DataFrames
batch_run.sh runs one script for seeds 1 to 5
paws_qqp.tsv PAWS-QQP: 677 question pairs, 191 of them duplicates (28 %); the OOD set for QQP
sampling.py, random_sampled_paws_qqp.tsv sampling.py draws 100 random pairs from paws_qqp.tsv (unseeded) into the second file; no other script reads either file
Efficient_LLM_Context_Distillation-CS_7643.pdf the report

Both RTE scripts work the same way:

  • Input: Premise: <sentence 1> Hypothesis: <sentence 2> ?, cut at 256 tokens.
  • The seed picks 16 training pairs from RTE's 2,490.
  • Learning rate 1e-5, 10 % warm-up, 40 epochs, gradient checkpointing.
  • After each epoch the model is scored on all 277 pairs of the RTE validation split (the code asks for 1,000 and caps at the split size) and on all 30,000 pairs of the HANS validation split. The checkpoint with the best RTE accuracy is kept.

One thing to know about pattern_based_ft_rte.py: it uses the class ids 0 and 1 directly as target token ids. In OPT's vocabulary those are <s> and <pad>, not word tokens such as " Yes" and " No" (ids 3216 and 440), so the model learns to answer with one of two special tokens. Its pct_target_tokens metric reports how often the prediction is one of them.

How to run

Use Python 3.11 and these versions. Both scripts ran end to end with them in October 2026, in a shortened test run (OPT-125m on CPU, one epoch, 64 HANS pairs):

python3.11 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.2.2 transformers==4.40.2 datasets==2.19.1 evaluate==0.4.2 accelerate==0.30.1 \
    numpy==1.26.4 pandas==2.2.3 pyarrow==16.1.0 scipy scikit-learn

Newer releases break the scripts. transformers 4.51 and later reject evaluation_strategy (5.0 also drops include_inputs_for_metrics). HANS loads through a dataset script: datasets 2.20 to 3.x run it only after asking (or with HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE=1), and datasets 4.0 and later refuse it.

python vanilla_ft_rte.py --model facebook/opt-125m --samples 16 --seed 1
python pattern_based_ft_rte.py -m facebook/opt-350m -n 16 -s 1
bash batch_run.sh vanilla_ft_rte.py facebook/opt-1.3b    # seeds 1 to 5

Each run writes models/rte/<method>/<model>_<n>-samples_<seed>-seed/: all_results.json (final metrics), training.log (metrics per epoch) and best_model/ (the kept checkpoint, 478 MB for OPT-125m). Git ignores models/. To collect finished runs:

from utils import get_data_from_approach
final, per_epoch = get_data_from_approach("rte", "vanilla_ft")  # or "pattern_based_ft"

The team ran on Georgia Tech's PACE-ICE cluster, Google Colab and personal machines. The report switched to Adafactor so the 1.3B model would fit in memory (section 2.8); the vanilla script here uses it at every size.

Who built what

Four Georgia Tech students did this project. The report lists them, and its Table 1 gives each person's part.

Saahil Sanganeriya (spelled Sanganeria in the report), who uploaded this repository in September 2025, wrote the RTE data and preprocessing scripts, implemented BitFit for RTE, ran the vanilla and PBFT experiments on every dataset at all three model sizes, and wrote the report's Approach section. The other three wrote the vanilla and PBFT training scripts, context distillation, in-context learning, BitFit, and the MNLI, QQP and HANS data scripts. They also ran those experiments, compiled the results, and wrote and edited the rest of the report. The two scripts here are the RTE versions of the team's vanilla and PBFT scripts.

Licence

There is no licence file. The code is the joint work of four students, so it is shared for reading and reference, not under an open-source licence.

References

  • Context distillation: A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment, arXiv:2112.00861.
  • PBFT, the few-shot protocol and the hyperparameters: Few-shot Fine-tuning vs. In-context Learning: A Fair Comparison and Evaluation, arXiv:2305.16938; code at uds-lsv/llmft.
  • BitFit: BitFit: Simple Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning for Transformer-based Masked Language-models, arXiv:2106.10199.
